details:
SPACE ARCHAEOLOGIST: THE FORGOTTEN MISSIONS

SPACE ARCHAEOLOGIST is an interactive educational web platform that explores the stories of NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating all such equipment as simply “abandoned” or “broken,” the project helps users understand what happened to each machine, why it remained on the planetary surface, and what scientific knowledge it helped generate.

The platform features six historical exhibits: Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity. Users can explore these exhibits, investigate six evidence-based cases, interview virtual machine personas, connect equipment to scientific discoveries through an interactive Science Constellation, and reconstruct selected mission timelines. A scoring and ranking system makes learning more engaging, while progress is saved in the browser.

The project's main benefit is that it transforms space history into an active learning experience. It encourages students to investigate evidence, understand scientific discoveries in context, distinguish between mission completion and equipment failure, and appreciate the engineering behind planetary exploration. Its intended impact is to make space science more accessible while promoting scientific curiosity, critical thinking and responsible exploration.

The project was developed using HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript. HTML provides the structure, CSS creates the responsive interface, and JavaScript powers the interactive exhibits, investigation cases, interviews, timelines and scoring system. Mission information and references are organised in a local JavaScript dataset, while browser LocalStorage saves user progress. The application is dependency-free and does not require a paid service or API key. Its machine interviews use a curated, knowledge-based question-and-answer system rather than claiming to be generative AI.

The project's creativity lies in combining a digital archive, an investigation game and conversational storytelling into one experience. Historical machines become the central characters, allowing users to approach scientific history from an unusual perspective: not just as observers of missions, but as investigators uncovering the legacy of the equipment.

During development, particular attention was given to historical accuracy, reliable NASA sources, accessibility, responsive design and scientific responsibility. The project distinguishes deliberately deployed equipment from machines that stopped functioning or lost communication. It also avoids presenting scientific evidence as proof of claims it cannot establish. The result is an engaging platform that shows that even when a mission ends, the knowledge it leaves behind continues to matter.
